newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - LLOYD'S ANNUAL VENTURES.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - LLOYD'S ANNUAL VENTURES.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
It's time Proteus paid attention to that little insurance operation in London's Lime Street known as Lloyd's, for quite a lot is going on.
Word has it that Lloyd's Syndicate Structure Working Party, due to report in the near future, is tending to come down on the side of ending the annual syndicate venture.

Arguments to and fro about the worth of the annual venture. Some say it is a remnant of the past which is impractical for modern planners and fund managers, others say it is the secret of the society's success.

However the drift of opinion is that as Lloyd's is reinventing itself in the wake of the lossmaking years, all practices perceived as archaic have to go. The only decision still to be made is whether to fade the annual venture out over time or to brush it a way in a revolution.
--oo0oo--

But some people can't wait. John Charman, deputy chairman of Lloyd's, has long favoured the revolution approach. This week he once again stirred up the debate on the future of names by moving to buy out the hundreds of remaining individual investors on all of his syndicates (469, 488 and 764).

High-rolling names who each invest more than 1 million stg say this is another sign that senior figures within the Lloyd's establishment want to push out the remaining 10,000 individual investors in the whole of the insurance market to make way for corporate capital.

Last week saw by Lloyd's that individual investors must in future lodge a larger deposit than previously. Instead of the original deposit of 25 per cent, this year the figure moves up to 32.5 per cent and will rise again next year to 35 per cent.
If the Syndicate Structure Working Part comes down against them, despite insistences that it will not make firm recommendations, names will have even more to worry about.
--oo0oo--

With this debate going on it is interesting to not as Christie Brockbank Shipton (CBS)points out that the underwriting results of the Lloyd's corporate investment trusts appear somewhat disappointing. Their average return is a meagre 9.23 per cent compared with 11.07 per cent from members Agent Pooling Arrangements (MAPA's). And these figures are before advisor and agent fees. CBS says even taking into account the extra 0.9 per cent that the corporate investors have to contribute ti the Central Fund, the supposedly highly sophisticated new investors do not appear to have beaten traditional members' agents at their own game.
--OO0OO--
